1.e4 Nc6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence
1.e4 Nc6.background: Named after Aron Nimzowitsch, who originated the defence and usually answered 2.d4 with 2...d5. Kasparov and Keene wrote that it “has never been fully accepted as a dependable opening”, though they considered it sound.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the full pawn centre at once, which is exactly what Black's last move invited. White gains space and the initiative, and Black has to prove that the centre can be undermined or restrained. This is the principled test of the whole defence.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Declined Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3.background: White players not eager for a theoretical battle on their opponent's turf often choose it.
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e5 while declining the fight on Black's own ground. If Black plays ...e5 the game becomes an ordinary open one, and avoiding that means choosing a less natural set-up. White keeps the d-pawn flexible and sidesteps prepared lines.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops and defends e4 without committing the d-pawn. Sound but unambitious: Black can occupy the centre with the e-pawn for an ordinary open game, or pick its own set-up, and White has no special edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Bb5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Pseudo-Spanish Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight, hoping for a well-known pressure game if Black fills the centre with ...e5. Until then the bishop achieves little, since nothing yet depends on the knight, and Black has several comfortable ways to avoid the transposition. An offbeat try, not a threat.

1.e4 Nc6 2.b4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Wheeler Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.b4.strategy: Offers the b-pawn to gain time for a broad centre. After ...Nxb4 White can drive the knight back with c3, but that leaves Black a clean pawn up in a solid position; the pawn is hard to justify.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes back at e4 immediately, so Black fights for the centre with a pawn and White must decide between closing, trading and defending. The cost is the knight on c6, which blocks the c-pawn and takes away the usual support for the d5 pawn.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5.background: The British grandmaster Tony Miles favoured this line.
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Attacks d4 a second time, so White must settle the centre now. Black gets a solid, easily developed game, but White keeps the extra space and decides how sharp it becomes, so it is sound but second-rate.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d6.strategy: Passive: Black solidly guards e5 and leaves the centre alone, conceding the initiative. White can take more space or develop at leisure while Black waits to undermine the centre later. Sound, but the easier game is White's.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 f6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Neo-Mongoloid Defence
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Prepares to hold the centre with a pawn, but takes the best square from the g8-knight and weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the e6 square. White gets a free hand in the centre while Black's pieces get in each other's way.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 a6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Woodchuck Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 a6.strategy: A waiting move that spends a tempo on a flank pawn and does nothing about White's centre. White can gain space with tempo against the c6 knight and keeps the initiative; nothing Black wants on the queenside is urgent yet.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Advance Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.e5.strategy: Gains space and keeps the pawn instead of trading, which closes the centre. White gets the larger share of space and a slight edge, while Black develops the bishop outside the pawn chain; the knight on c6 takes away the usual c-pawn break against White's chain.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Resolves the tension and clears the way for the pieces. Only the queen can recapture at once, so it comes out early and can be chased with tempo, but it also hits d4 together with the knight, which keeps the game balanced.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 and pressures d5, offering a pawn in the centre: if Black takes on e4, a central pawn push attacks the c6 knight and gains time. Black has to choose between grabbing the pawn and holding the tension.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Be3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Hornung Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Be3.strategy: Defends d4 and develops, but leaves the e4 pawn unprotected, so Black can take it with ...dxe4. White then has to prove that the lead in development pays for the pawn. Playable, but it asks White to play for compensation that the other moves do not need.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Exchange Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: The natural recapture: Black wins the pawn back at once, and the queen hits d4 together with the knight, so White must defend it or give it up. The queen comes out early and can be chased by development, but Black's pieces come out easily and equality is within reach.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Nb4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Aachen Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Nb4.strategy: A gambit: the knight heads for d5, but it spends a second move on the same piece. White can challenge it with a developing bishop check, keeps the extra pawn and has the better of the game.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Hangs the knight: the pawn on d5 already attacks it, so White takes on c6 and wins a piece for a pawn. Black has not won the pawn back either. The plain recapture with the queen is the way.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Exchange Variation, Marshall Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3.strategy: Gains a tempo on the queen by developing, but leaves d4 to its fate: Black can take it and White must prove that the lead in development is worth a pawn. If Black merely retreats the queen, White has gained a tempo for free. A risky, speculative choice.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops and defends d4 a second time, so White threatens to gain a tempo on the queen with Nc3 without losing the centre pawn. White keeps the lead in development and the better pawn structure, and Black has to find a way to hit the centre to hold the balance.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Be3.strategy: Defends d4 with a developing move, so the knight can then come to c3 with tempo on the queen and the pawn stays safe. White keeps a small, lasting initiative and Black gets quick development to compensate; a sound way to play for a slight edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the offered pawn and accepts the challenge. White's natural answer chases the c6 knight with a central pawn push, so the game becomes Black's extra pawn against White's time and activity, and Black aims to develop quickly and soundly.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Vehre Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4 a second time, but White does not have to defend: 4.e5 attacks the knight, which must retreat or be traded off. White gains space and time, and Black stays awkward, since the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 a6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Brandics Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 a6.strategy: Neither takes nor supports anything and offers the d5 pawn, intending to win it back by hitting it with pieces. The a-pawn also denies White a check on b5. Offbeat and playable, but White gets the choice and the easier game.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Erben Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6.strategy: Ignores the tension and fianchettoes, so White can take on d5 and keep the pawn for now. Black hopes to win it back with piece play, but development lags while the extra pawn is real.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 e5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Heinola-Deppe Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 e5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once and offers a pawn. If White takes on e5, ...d4 hits the c3 knight and Black wins the pawn back with active, open play. Playable, but White can choose which pawn to take and keeps a small edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5.name: Dunst Opening: Berlin Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5.strategy: Gains space with tempo by hitting the c6 knight, which must move. The pawn on d5 cramps Black's pieces and gives White the choice between regaining the e4 pawn at once and playing for a lead in development.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Be3.strategy: Defends d4 twice and develops, but leaves the e4 pawn alone. Black can often keep the extra pawn by supporting it with a developing move or a pawn, so White must prove that the lead in development pays for it.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.Nge2.strategy: Develops and adds a defender to d4, so the centre pawn is safe, and prepares to bring the knight to g3 to hit e4 a second time. It is slow: Black is a pawn up and has time to support it and finish development.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Nimzowitsch Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5.strategy: The main reply: the knight steps into the centre, out of the pawn's reach, and eyes f3, d3 and c4. Black keeps the extra pawn for now, while White gets time with development against the knight; Black is close to equality.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Nb8.strategy: Retreats to the starting square, which avoids any harassment of the knight but undoes the development. Black keeps the pawn, but the knight is passive, White's d5 pawn cramps Black's position, and White is happy to use the lost time.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Nb4.strategy: Goes for the d5 pawn and the c2 square, but the knight has no good square afterwards: a3 chases it, it cannot return to c6 because the pawn takes it, and it ends on the rim. White regains the e4 pawn with a lead in time.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Nb8 5.f.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Scandinavian Variation, Bogoljubow Variation, Richter Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Nb8 5.f.strategy: Attacks the e4 pawn at once, offering to open lines for it: if Black takes, White recaptures with a developing move and has a lead in development. Black is a pawn up and solid, so White needs real activity as payment; risky but playable.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Nb8 5.N.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once: Black has no way to hold it, and the pawn on d5 stays protected by the queen. Material is level, White keeps the extra space and Black has lost two tempi with the knight, so Black has to complete development against a cramping pawn.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Nb8 5.B.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and keeps the knight's pressure on e4, but does not take the pawn. Black can defend it with a developing move, and White must then prove that the lead in development is worth the pawn.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn and trades the centre away. If the knight recaptures, the game opens, pieces come off quickly and White keeps a small, safe edge, with the d-file half-open against Black's d7 pawn. Black must be content with a plain, slightly worse game.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.d5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Linksspringer Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.d5.strategy: Pushes the pawn past the attack, gaining space and driving the knight from its fine post on c6. The centre closes into a manoeuvring game where White's extra room is the asset, though it brings only a slight plus in practice, and Black's knight needs time to find a new job.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.Nf3.strategy: Defends d4 and develops instead of settling the tension. If Black takes on d4, White recaptures with a piece and has an open centre and a lead in development; otherwise the game stays level. Sound, but it settles for equality where pushing the pawn or taking on e5 keeps a small plus.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5.strategy: The natural recapture: material is level and the knight stands in the centre, where White will try to harry it with tempo. Black gets a healthy pawn structure and a solid game, and accepts having to defend a little more passively.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Bc5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Bielefelder Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Bc5.strategy: Develops with the bishop aimed at f2 instead of winning the e5 pawn back, hoping a lead in development pays for it. White can protect the pawn with a developing move and stay a clean pawn up, so Black has to prove that the activity is worth the material.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 f6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Hammer Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 f6.strategy: Tries to undermine the e5 pawn at once, but the f-pawn leaves the diagonal in front of the king: a queen check on h5 is possible immediately. White is a pawn up, and Black's weakened king is too high a price for the attempt to win it back.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Qh4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Herford Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Qh4.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hit the e4 pawn, which is undefended for the moment, and eyes f2. White can defend with a developing move and stay a pawn up, so Black has spent a queen move for nothing, and a queen exposed in the centre becomes a target for tempo moves.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 d6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, de Smet Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 d6.strategy: Offers the d-pawn to open lines for both bishops. White simply takes it and Black, after recapturing, is a clean pawn down with a lead in development. That is too little against a sound setup, and White has few weaknesses to attack.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nf3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Paulsen Attack
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nf3.strategy: The calm, principled choice: it develops and attacks the knight on e5 at once. Knights are likely to trade, leaving White with the better development and the half-open d-file against d7, in a quiet game that offers a small, low-risk edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.f4.strategy: Kicks the knight at once and builds a strong pawn centre with a gain of tempo. White takes space and sets the agenda, but the advance weakens the e1-h4 diagonal and the king's cover, so the centre has to be defended with care.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Keres Attack
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 and develops, but does nothing about the knight on e5, which Black can settle at once, and then pin the knight on c3 with the bishop. White has a sound, flexible position and gives up the chance to play for an edge by harrying the centralised knight.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.f4 Ng6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Main Line
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.f4 Ng6.strategy: Retreats to a safe square from which the knight eyes f4 and h4. White has gained space and tempo, so Black's task is to undermine the strong pawn centre; the knight is well placed for that, though another pawn advance can drive it away again.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.f4 Nc6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Kennedy Variation, Riemann Defence
1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.f4 Nc6.strategy: Goes back to c6, undoing Black's two knight moves: White got the pawn centre with a free tempo. Black keeps a solid position, but has lost time, with no obvious way to challenge the centre soon.

1.e4 Nc6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.f4 Qh4+.strategy: A check that wins nothing: the g-pawn blocks it and attacks the queen while the f-pawn still attacks the knight, and Black cannot save both. Black ends up a piece down.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 and develops, but the pressure is hollow: the knight on c3 already defends the pawn, and White can build a full pawn centre at once. The knight on c6 gets in the way of Black's c-pawn, so the set-up stays awkward and White chooses how the game goes.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 e6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: French Connection
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a solid pawn structure, but the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn, so the usual break against White's centre is missing. Playable, but Black has made a harder version of the structure for itself.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the bishop and pressure the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. The knight on c6 is committed early, and White can build a full pawn centre without hindrance; Black must wait for a chance to challenge it.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn that the knight on c6 already guards, and steers the game into a classical open game with an even fight. Black gives up the unbalancing character of the opening but loses nothing, though White decides how sharp it becomes.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: A compact defence: the pawn controls e5, opens the bishop on c8 and keeps Black's position sound. Black concedes the centre without attacking it, so White gets space and the choice of plans, and Black waits for a chance to challenge later.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks e4 and invites White to push the pawn and gain space with tempo, in the hope of undermining the advanced pawn later. The knight already on c6 adds little to that plan, and White gets the space at no cost.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Franco-Nimzowitsch Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Builds a solid pawn structure and prepares ...d5, but the knight on c6 blocks the c-pawn and takes away the usual break against White's centre. Playable, though White gets a freer game than in the normal version of the structure.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Colorado Countergambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5.background: Played with some success by the American international master Doug Root and more recently by the Finnish IM Olli Salmensuu, among others. Eric Schiller, who also calls it the Lean Variation, describes it as "fierce" and for "thrill-seekers".
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Strikes at e4 from the flank, hoping to open lines and get ...d5 in. It weakens Black's own king, and White can simply take the pawn. Black can usually win the material back, but pays for it with a permanently loosened kingside.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre, with the pawn already guarded by the knight on c6, and offers the transposition to a classical open game. Black gives up the unusual character of the opening in exchange for a standard, equal position with no concessions.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Colorado Countergambit Accepted
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5 3.exf5.strategy: Takes the pawn, which also removes the e-pawn from the centre. Black cannot recapture at once, so the choice is whether to hold the extra pawn or hand it back for a comfortable game. The f-pawn is gone for good, so Black's kingside stays weakened.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move instead of taking the pawn, which lets Black off. Black takes on e4 and White recaptures, so material is level, the gambit has cost Black nothing and Black has a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 f5 3.e5.strategy: Pushes past the pawn to gain space, but Black can strike at e5 at once and the pawn becomes a target. White has not won the f5 pawn, so the gambit has cost Black nothing, while White's own centre pawn is the one under attack.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5.strategy: Gains space and attacks the knight in one move. The pawn is attacked by the knight on c6 and guarded by Nf3, so White gets a central space advantage that Black must try to undermine, or else be cramped.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the pawn centre intact, but it gives up the space gain of the e-pawn push. Black can set up a symmetrical open game in which every piece develops naturally, so White gets a solid position and no edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.d3.strategy: Guards e4 with a pawn and keeps the position closed and flexible, but it blocks the c1-bishop and leaves the centre to Black. Black can meet it with ...e5 and equalise comfortably, so White gets a quiet game with little prospect of an edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.background: Invented by the Spanish grandmaster Marc Narciso Dublan, who called it "El Columpio" ("The Swing").
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight again to hit e5 a second time. The idea is risky: White guards the pawn with a central move, and the knight, which has moved twice, will probably end up on the rim while White keeps the space and an edge.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nd5.strategy: Moves the attacked knight to the centre rather than the rim and leaves the knight on c6 to keep pressure on the advanced pawn. White has gained space and will use it, but the e-pawn is also a target, and Black plays to show that White has overextended.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ne4.strategy: Puts the knight where a pawn hits it at once: 4.d3 gains a tempo, the knight has only one retreat, and it is chased again by d4. Black has spent several moves on the same piece and White builds a broad pawn centre at leisure.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Nxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn with the c6-knight, but Nf3 takes it back. Black is a piece down for a pawn or two (...Nxe4 follows) and has nothing to show for it.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn, so that it is guarded by pawn and knight against the two attackers. White builds a strong pawn centre, and Black's knight has used up its time.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.Qe2.strategy: Holds e5 with the queen, but this passes up the strong pawn centre: the queen blocks the f1-bishop and Black can hit e5 a third time with ...d6, so the knight's adventure costs Black far less than it should.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.h3.strategy: Attacks the knight at once but forgets that e5 is attacked twice and defended once: 4...Ngxe5 takes the pawn, and after 5.Nxe5 Nxe5 White has lost a pawn for nothing.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6.strategy: Attacks e5 a third time, with knight, knight and pawn, and opens the c8-bishop. White's advanced pawn is now attacked three times and guarded twice, so White must act at once, and Black has found the real point of the knight's journey.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 e6.strategy: Backs the centre with a pawn and keeps a solid structure, but it leaves the c8-bishop hemmed in and does nothing about the cramp: e5 is attacked twice and defended twice, so White keeps the space and can harass the knight at leisure.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 f6.strategy: Attacks e5 a third time with a pawn, but loosens e6 and the king's diagonal and leaves the knight on g4 with few good squares: 5.h3 drives it away, and Black ends up at least a pawn down with the worse game.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Chases the knight and so removes one of the three pieces attacking e5. White spends a pawn move on it but gains time, because the knight has to go to the edge of the board and Black's counterplay thins out.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.ex.strategy: Gives up the pawn that cramps Black: after the exchange the knight on g4 is left undisturbed and Black recaptures with an easy game. The space advantage that 5.h3 keeps is gone.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.Bb.strategy: Pins the knight on c6 against the king, but the knight on g4 is left undisturbed and Black can take on e5, so the pin gives White less than chasing the knight does. White is still a little better, but has let the best moment pass.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: The only sensible retreat: the others lose the knight or give it up for a pawn. It stands on the rim, but it still covers f5 and f7, and the pressure on e5 remains. Black has to accept a slightly worse position.
Takes the pawn with the attacked knight, but the exchanges on e5 leave Black a knight down for two pawns with no attack to show for it.
A sacrifice that does not work: the king takes the knight and Black has only a pawn for the piece. White's king steps out, but Black has no developed pieces to exploit it.
Goes back to the square the knight came from, where the e5 pawn takes it: Black has lost a piece for a pawn.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence, Exchange Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Removes the attacked pawn by exchange and so eases the tension in the centre. Black's recapture leaves a simple position in which the knight on h6 is still misplaced, and White keeps the better development and the safer game.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence, Pin Variation
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Pins the knight on c6 against the king, so it cannot move. This takes it out of the fight for e5 and d4, and the bishop can capture it and double Black's pawns. White keeps the better pawn centre and the initiative.

1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: El Columpio Defence, El Columpio Gambit
1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e5 Ng4 4.d4 d6 5.h3.strategy: Offers a pawn to open lines for the pieces. It can simply be taken, leaving Black a clean pawn up, and White's compensation is little more than the bishop on c1 aimed at the knight on h6 to damage Black's kingside pawns.

Develops the queen's knight and adds to the pressure without hurry: e5 is already guarded as often as it is attacked, so Black has nothing to win there. White keeps the space and the better development while the knight on h6 stays misplaced on the rim.
